In a structured product, the issuer combines two elements: (1) a Zero Coupon NID that pays RM1,000,000 at maturity; and (2) a call option on the KLCI. The investor pays RM900,000 upfront. Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies how the RM900,000 is allocated between the two components?
RM900,000 entirely to buy the call option.
RM900,000 is split exactly 50:50 between the ZNID and the call option.
Most of the RM900,000 goes to purchase the ZNID at a discount (e.g., RM860,000).
The RM900,000 goes entirely to the ZNID.

Answer: C — Most of the RM900,000 goes to purchase the ZNID at a discount (e.g., RM860,000). Why this is correct:
The classic principal-protected structured product split: The PV of the ZNID equals approximately RM860,000 (growing to RM1,000,000 at maturity — this is the capital protection component). Remaining = RM900,000 - RM860,000 = RM40,000 (less any issuer fees) → used to buy the call option (the equity upside component). The ZNID is purchased at a deep discount; the difference between the purchase price and par represents the return of principal guarantee. The option budget is whatever is left after funding the ZNID and covering fees. This split is the foundation of ALL principal-protected structured product design. Why the other options are wrong:
A — RM900,000 entirely to buy the call option; ZNID is provided free under the product terms. It misstates the product structure, payoff, legal documentation or risk exposure.
B — RM900,000 is split exactly 50:50 between the ZNID and the call option under the product terms. It misstates the product structure, payoff, legal documentation or risk exposure.
D — The RM900,000 goes entirely to the ZNID; the call option is purchased using the issuer's profits under the product terms. It misstates the product structure, payoff, legal documentation or risk exposure. Exam cue: Structured-product questions test conditional protection, issuer/counterparty risk, participation/payoff formula, legal documents, early-exit risk and the fixed-income leg plus derivative/option leg.

An analyst at a stockbroking firm prepares a research report on a bond. The report contains a factual error: it states the bond matures in 2030 when it actually matures in 2025. A client relies on the report and buys the bond expecting a 2030 maturity. Which CMSA provision is MOST directly engaged?

Section 178.

Section 92A.

Section 92A covers wilful omissions — but if the misstatement was inadvertent, Section 92 (reasonable basis) is also engaged because any recommendation based on incorrect fundamental data (wrong maturity) cannot have had a reasonable basis. Why the other options are wrong:
A — Section 232 — prospectus requirements under the CMSA provision. It points to a different CMSA duty, section or consequence.

Formula: Put intrinsic value = max(strike price − current price, 0).

Which statement correctly describes best execution?
Best execution means proprietary trades always come first instead of matching the correct market role.
Client instructions are irrelevant to execution instead of matching the correct market role.
Unclear language is preferred instead of matching the correct market role.
Dealers and brokers should execute client orders promptly and fairly, following specific client instructions where applicable.

Answer: D — Dealers and brokers should execute client orders promptly and fairly, following specific client instructions where applicable.
Why this is correct:
Market-participant roles must be kept separate. Brokers arrange or execute for clients, dealers may trade/quote for clients or own account, rating agencies assess credit risk, arbitragers exploit price discrepancies, and speculators take directional risk.
Why the other options are wrong:
A — Best execution means proprietary trades always come first when dealing with the client when fair dealing standards are applied. This confuses one market participant's role with another.
B — Client instructions are irrelevant to execution when dealing with the client when fair dealing standards are applied. This confuses one market participant's role with another.
C — Unclear language is preferred when markets are volatile when dealing with the client when fair dealing standards are applied. This confuses one market participant's role with another.
Exam cue: Eliminate options that assign the role to the wrong party, use an absolute claim or reverse the tested rule.

When should yield to call be especially relevant for a callable bond?
When the bond has no embedded option and can only be redeemed at final maturity.
When the investor controls the issuer and can force redemption at any time.
When the issuer has a call option and may redeem the bond before final maturity.
When the instrument is a short-term Treasury bill issued at a discount.

Answer: C - When the issuer has a call option and may redeem the bond before final maturity.
Why this is correct:
Yield to call is relevant when a callable bond may be redeemed by the issuer before the stated maturity date. Investors use it to assess the return if the bond is called at the call date and call price instead of being held to final maturity.

A is wrong because a bond with no embedded call option is normally assessed using yield to maturity.
B is wrong because the call right belongs to the issuer, not the investor.
D is wrong because Treasury bills are discount money-market instruments and do not involve callable-bond analysis.
Exam cue: Callable bond = issuer call right; puttable bond = investor put right; YTC matters when early issuer redemption is plausible.

Which option is consistent with the applicable rule treatment of callable bonds?
The investor controls the issuer’s call option for the same bond.
The bond must always be called.
Calling the bond removes reinvestment risk for the investor for the same bond.
A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under stated call terms.

Answer: D — A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under stated call terms.
Why this is correct:
A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under the call terms. Issuers are more likely to call when rates fall, which creates reinvestment risk for investors.

A — The investor controls the issuer’s call option for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
B — The bond must always be called when rates rise for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
C — Calling the bond removes reinvestment risk for the investor for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
Exam cue: Call = right to buy; put = right to sell; buyer has a right, writer has an obligation.

Bond price = present value of coupon payments + present value of par value.

Apply the participation formula to RM150,000, 60% participation and a 10% underlying gain.
RM150,000 only because participation removes upside.
RM159,000 total proceeds, before costs and tax.
RM165,000 total proceeds.
RM9,000 total proceeds.
Maturity proceeds = protected principal + (principal × participation rate × underlying gain).

Answer: B — RM159,000 total proceeds, before costs and tax.
Why this is correct:
Formula: Maturity proceeds = protected principal + (principal × participation rate × underlying gain).
Working:
Participation-linked return = RM150,000 × 60% × 10% = RM9,000. Maturity proceeds = RM150,000 + RM9,000 = RM159,000.
Why the other options are wrong:
A — RM150,000 only because participation removes upside: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
C — RM165,000 total proceeds: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
D — RM9,000 total proceeds: uses the principal only, applies the full underlying gain without participation, or treats the return as the total proceeds.
Exam cue: For principal-protected participation payoffs, calculate the upside return, then add it to principal.

In relation to callable bonds, which statement is correct in a compliance review?
A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under stated call terms.
The investor controls the issuer’s call option for the same bond.
The bond must always be called.
Calling the bond removes reinvestment risk for the investor for the same bond.

Answer: A — A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under stated call terms.

A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem before maturity under the call terms. Issuers are more likely to call when rates fall, which creates reinvestment risk for investors.

B — The investor controls the issuer’s call option for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
C — The bond must always be called when rates rise for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
D — Calling the bond removes reinvestment risk for the investor for the same bond. This reverses or misapplies the bond pricing, yield, duration, credit-risk or call-risk rule.
Exam cue: Eliminate options that assign the role to the wrong party, use an absolute claim or reverse the tested rule.
